mention.lead_sentence: we suggest that the user swirl his hands counter-clockwise with respect to the faucet as shown in Figure 1

items.note: A cross-section cartoon rather than a plot: a black outline bathtub seen from the side with the faucet at the upper right, a stick figure standing in it whose arm is drawn as two straight lines reaching into the water, and two thick red circular arrows showing the counter-clockwise swirl the text asks for. The water is filled with a red-to-blue gradient that runs from the faucet side to the far side - the temperature gradient the swirl is meant to remove - although nothing on the drawing states this and no scale, axis or legend exists. It is the only exhibit in the paper that is a drawing of an action rather than a plot of a measurement, and the only one whose caption prints below it as a numbered figure in the body chapters.

Three cooling series measured in 100 mL, 300 mL and 800 mL beakers, drawn as marker-plus-line curves over 0 to 62 min, ordinate 20 to 100 degrees Celsius, title 'Water Beaker Cooling', legend at the top right INSIDE the axes with entries '100mL', '300mL Beaker' and '800mL Beaker'. The three markers differ (open circle, triangle, cross) but the legend's first entry drops the word 'Beaker' that the other two keep, and no caption, number or pointer in the body text identifies the exhibit - the surrounding sentence only says 'We created a graph to represent the data'.

The same three beaker series re-plotted from a spreadsheet as thick marker lines with three thin dotted fit curves overlaid, title 'Water Beaker Temperature vs. Time Regression', ordinate 0 to 90 degrees Celsius, legend OUTSIDE the frame on the right with six entries: the three data series and 'Expon. (800mL)', 'Expon. (300mL)', 'Expon. (100mL)'. Three fit labels print inside the plot at the right, each reading 'Y = 77e^-0.029x', 'Y = 77e^-0.052x' and 'Y = 77e^-0.036x' with R squared 0.9694, 0.9092 and 0.8528. THE PRINTED FIT EQUATIONS ARE NOT THE PAPER'S EQUATIONS: (8), (9) and (10) on the next page all read y = 77e^-knx + 23, and the asymptote constant 23 is missing from all three labels here, so the plot's own labels imply the water cools towards 0 degrees and not towards the 23 degree room.

The team's own bathtub experiment: a single marker line falling from 37.0 to 33.2 degrees Celsius over 0 to 62 min, title 'Temperature vs. Time for Real-World Bathtub Experiment', ordinate 33 to 37.5 degrees Celsius, one-entry legend 'temp' outside the frame at the right. This is the only absolute-temperature curve of the paper's own data and the only one where the y-axis span is small enough to show the measurement wobble - the series steps down in flat runs of three or four points between readings.

The same experiment re-plotted after the 21 degree offset: the series now runs from 16.05 to 12.4 over the same 0 to 62 min, with a dotted exponential fit labelled 'Y = 16.00000e^-0.00448x / R squared 0.97326' and a two-entry legend ('temp', 'Expon. (temp)') outside the frame. THE AXIS STILL SAYS TEMPERATURE IN DEGREES CELSIUS AND THE TITLE IS WORD FOR WORD THE ONE ABOVE: the shifted quantity T minus 21 is plotted against a temperature axis, so the exhibit shows 37 degree bath water sitting at 16 degrees and nothing on the page says the 21 degrees were subtracted. The offset itself disagrees with the beakers' 23 degrees, and equation (24) on p18 restores it as +21 while the beaker constants are +23 with no explanation of the difference.

Four open circles and a fitted power curve, title 'K-value Regression', ordinate K from 0.00 to 0.04, abscissa 'V^2/SA^3' from 0 to 140000, and the label 'R squared: 0.99764' printed inside the frame at the top right. No legend, no gridline, no unit on K. The four points are the team's bathtub experiment plus the three beakers, and the whole of section 4.2.2's model selection rests on them - which is why the next three pages print the same four points three more times against three other transforms of the same predictor.

The same four points and the same fit against the SQUARED predictor: abscissa '(V^2/SA^3)^2' with ticks in scientific notation 0.0e+00 to 1.5e+10, ordinate K 0.00 to 0.04, title 'K-value Regression' again, label 'R squared: 0.996529' inside the frame. Nothing in the drawing distinguishes it from the exhibit one page earlier except the abscissa ticks: the points sit in the same order, the curve has the same shape, and the two pages are otherwise identical screenshots.

The third copy: the same four points against 'square root of (V^2/SA^3)', ticks 50 to 350, ordinate K 0.00 to 0.04, title 'K-value Regression', 'R squared: 0.999294' inside the frame. The text between the two exhibits says 'Seeing as this is worse, we test ...' and then 'Noticing improvement, we test ...', so the reader is asked to compare three regressions whose only difference is a tick-label string.

The fourth and last: the same four points against 'cubic root of V^2/SA^3', ticks 20 to 50, ordinate K 0.00 to 0.04, title 'K-value Regression', 'R squared: 0.999299' inside the frame. This one is the model the paper adopts, and its regression is reported in the body as 'R2 = 0.99929854436231100000' - twenty significant digits for four data points, and one more digit than the 0.999299 the same page's exhibit prints.

Deviance against flow rate for the standard tub: one red curve on a unitless ordinate (Deviance, 200 to 1800) against 'Flow Rate (GPM)' 1.0 to 16.0, title 'Optimal Flow Rate (SA: 1800, V: 25200)', and an unframed legend OUTSIDE-LEFT with two entries, 'Bathtub' and 'Minimum'. THE MINIMUM THE LEGEND PROMISES IS NOT VISIBLE: the text tells the reader the answer is 'represented by the point indicated at the bottom of the graph, at (1.81, 10.179381314125882)', but no marker, crosshair or label appears at that point or anywhere else in the axes, and the appendix's own code shows why - it adds the 'Minimum' entry as a single point carrying its value, and that point sits at the curve's floor, at or below the frame's lowest tick, so the one number the method minimizes is the one the chart cannot place. The ordinate has no zero tick either.

The simulated bath at the chosen flow rate: open circles falling from 37.5 to 35.6 degrees Celsius, ordinate 'Temperature (degrees Celsius)' 36.0 to 37.5 with the frame extending below the lowest tick, abscissa 'Time (minutes)' 0 to 40, title 'Temperature vs. Time @ Optimal Flow Rate 1.81GPM'. No legend, no marker on the point where the faucet turns on. The claim it illustrates - that the curve stops falling and turns back up once 1.4 degrees have been lost - is not visible: the series is a nearly straight decay with no turn, and the title's '@' and the run-together '1.81GPM' are the only text on it.

Simulation against experiment: open circles with a straight fit line over 0 to 40 min, ordinate 34.5 to 37.0 degrees Celsius, title 'Validation of Experiment', and 'R squared: 0.999836.' printed inside the frame - the trailing full stop is part of the label. No legend and no key to say which mark is the simulation and which the experiment, which matters because the section's claim is that the two cannot be told apart.

An Autodesk Inventor render of the standard 60 by 30 by 14 inch tub, printed alone on its page: grey shaded surfaces with soft shadows and no annotation of any kind - no dimension line, no axis, no scale bar, no label, not even the design's name, which appears only in the prose of the following page. The drawing is the only place the shape of this design exists, and nothing on it can be measured or matched to the surface area and volume the text quotes beside it.

items.note: The seven designs collapsed into one picture: three open circles of optimal flow rate against surface area, title 'Constant Volume', abscissa 'Surface Area (sq.in)' 1600 to 1800, ordinate 'Optimal Flow Rate (GPM)' 1.5 to 4.5. No legend, no labels on the points, no line. Three points cannot support the section's claim that the flow rate 'decreases, but then increases again, following no set pattern', and two of the seven designs are missing from the plot entirely - the standard tub at 1800 sq.in and the fiberglass and bubble-bath runs are the only ones near this abscissa range.

The volume sweep: four open circles of optimal flow rate against volume, title 'Constant Surface Area', abscissa 'Volume (cubic in)' 18000 to 24000, ordinate 1.4 to 2.0, with one marker sitting above the highest labelled tick. No legend, no point labels. Like its twin above it, the exhibit is titled with the quantity that is held fixed rather than the one that varies, so the two plots are named for their constants and the reader has to read the abscissa to learn which is which.

The fiberglass run: deviance against flow rate, title 'Optimal Flow Rate (SA: 2340, V: 25200)', ordinate 1000.0 to 4000.0, outside-left legend 'Bathtub' and 'Minimum'. The ordinate is an order of magnitude above every other chart's, which is the point - the tub loses heat fast enough that its best flow rate is 7.52 gallons per minute - but the 'Minimum' entry is again undrawn, and the title's surface area, 2340 sq.in, is not the 6120 sq.in the text derives one page earlier for the same run.

The bubble-bath run: deviance against flow rate, title 'Optimal Flow Rate (SA: 1710, V: 25200)', ordinate 100.0 to 1400.0, outside-left legend 'Bathtub' and 'Minimum'. The title's 1710 sq.in is the arithmetic of the section - 1800 square inches of water surface multiplied by the assumed 0.95 insulation factor - so this is the one deviance chart whose title can be checked against the text and agrees with it. Two of the frame's gridlines are drawn heavier than the rest.

note:
Paper 95, Team 54164, the bathtub heat-loss paper with a home-made diffuser at the end. Forty-four
pages, thirty-five measured regions on thirty-two of them, resolving into THIRTY-FIVE FIGURE ROWS,
NO TABLE ROW and NO EXCLUSION. Unaccounted zero. The paper prints no table at all: not a constants
table, not a symbol table, not a results table, and every one of the thirty-five exhibits is a plot,
a render or a product picture.

The overwhelming fact about this paper's exhibits is that thirty-one of the thirty-five carry no
caption and no number. The four that do are Figures 1 to 4, and three of those are the closing
product pictures; the only captioned exhibit in the body chapters is Figure 1, a cartoon. Everything
else - twenty-one spreadsheet and MATLAB screenshots and eight Inventor renders - is dropped into the
page with whatever title the plotting tool drew inside its own frame, or with nothing at all. The
renders have no label of any kind, so the only thing that identifies a design is the dimension
paragraph that follows its page.

Citation is even thinner than captioning. Only Figure 1 is ever named by a sentence, and that
sentence is on the abstract page, five pages before the exhibit prints: "we suggest that the user
swirl his hands counter-clockwise with respect to the faucet as shown in Figure 1". Figures 2, 3 and
4 are never named at all, and the other thirty-one exhibits are pointed at, when they are pointed at,
by bare phrases that name no figure: "We created a graph to represent the data", "The results of our
experiment are as follows", "Comparing the deviance of every flow rate produces the following",
"The following is a temperature vs. time graph". A reader who wants to know which chart is which has
to read the in-plot titles, which is the only reason the paper is legible.

Section 5 is a template run eight times. Seven alternative tub designs are each given exactly two
exhibits - an unlabelled Inventor render alone on its page, then a deviance-against-flow-rate chart
on the next page whose title is the only identification - plus the standard tub, whose deviance chart
is printed TWICE, once on p16 as section 4.3.1's flow-rate selection and again on p20 as 5.1's first
case, with the identical title "Optimal Flow Rate (SA: 1800, V: 25200)". All eight charts share one
recipe: abscissa "Flow Rate (GPM)" 1.0 to 16.0, a unitless "Deviance" ordinate whose limits change
from chart to chart (2-32 for the square tub up to 1000-4000 for the fiberglass run), and an unframed
outside-left legend with two entries, "Bathtub" and "Minimum". No minimum point is visible in any of
the eight. The appendix explains the absence: the plotting code appends the second series as a single
point carrying its value, so the minimum is drawn at the curve's own floor - and in three of the eight
charts that floor lies below the frame's lowest tick, which is why the text can tell the reader the
answer is "the point indicated at the bottom of the graph, at (1.81, 10.179381314125882)" while the
graph shows no such point.

The four k-value regressions (pp12-14) are the same four data points plotted four times against four
transforms of one predictor - V^2/SA^3, its square, its square root and its cube root - with
R squared 0.99764, 0.996529, 0.999294 and 0.999299 printed inside the frames. Nothing in the four
screenshots distinguishes them except tick labels, and the paper adopts the last one and reports its
fit as "R2 = 0.99929854436231100000" - twenty significant digits from four points.

Two plotting defects change what the exhibits say. The three exponential fits printed on p10 read
"Y = 77e^-0.029x" with no asymptote constant, while equations (8) to (10) on p11 all read
"y = 77e^-knx + 23": the plot's own labels imply the water cools to 0 degrees instead of the 23
degree room. And p11's second plot is the SAME experiment after the offset has been subtracted -
37 degrees of bath water appearing at 16 degrees - still against an axis labelled "Temperature
[degrees Celsius]" and still under the identical title "Temperature vs. Time for Real-World Bathtub
Experiment"; the constant is restored as +21 in equation (24), not the +23 the beakers use, and the
paper never mentions the difference.

Design and rendering: the eight Inventor renders carry no dimension, no scale bar, no axis and no
name, and are printed one per page at full page height; the blueprint of Figure 2 is pasted as a
low-resolution screenshot of a drawing sheet, with the smallest dimension callouts illegible at
printed size; Figures 3 and 4 are renderings rather than photographs and are not drawn to the same
scale as the blueprint. The scatter on p35 has three points and is titled with the quantity that is
held constant, as is the four-point scatter on p36, so the pair is named for its constants and the
abscissae have to be read to tell them apart.

Families: line 16, surface-or-3D 8, scatter 7, photo-or-raster-image 3, flowchart-or-schematic 1.
rules: Measure first, then read the pixels: thirty-five measured regions resolve into thirty-five figure rows, no table row and no exclusion, and no region is counted twice [place.page_order].

Thirty-one of the thirty-five exhibits print NO caption and NO number: only Figures 1 to 4 are captioned, so every other row records caption_source 'none' and numbering 'none' while the four captioned rows take the printed 'Figure N:' form [caption.numbering].

The plotting program's own title is not a caption: an uncaptioned chart keeps whatever title Excel or MATLAB drew inside the frame ('Optimal Flow Rate (SA: 1800, V: 25200)'), that title is recorded in the note and in the geometry, and no caption block is invented from it [caption.verbatim].

A bare pointer is not a citation: the paper says 'We created a graph', 'Comparing the deviance of every flow rate produces the following' and 'The following constructions were rendered using Autodesk Inventor', and none of those names a figure, so thirty-four rows are uncited and only Figure 1 is named (on the abstract page, five pages before it prints) [mention.count].

An exhibit printed alone on a page with no text is placed by the section that precedes it: the eight Inventor renders sit on textless pages and belong to the design whose dimensions the following page states, which is the page order 5.1 and 5.2 run through [mention.lead_pages].

Two regions hold the same plot: p16 and p20 print the standard tub's deviance chart twice, with the same title and the same axes, and both are recorded as rows because both are printed exhibits [place.doc_order].

A figure block with no caption, no axis and no label is still an exhibit when the paper prints it as one: the eight Inventor renders are rows, not exclusions, because each occupies its whole page and is referred to by the surrounding prose as a design [place.area_frac].
Section placement follows the heading index, which indexed every heading this paper prints; the paths quote the labels the index gives [place.section_path].
